# Bahuvedanīya Sutta (MN 59 (PTS MN i 396))

**ID:** MN 59 (PTS MN i 396)

**Title (Pali):** Bahuvedanīya Sutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bahuvedanīya Sutta* ("The Many Kinds of Feeling", MN 59) is the 59th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya. Set in Sāvatthī, the text originates in a dispute between the monk Udāyi and the carpenter Pañcakaṅga regarding the enumeration and classification of feelings (*vedanā*) [Klaus & Hartmann 2007]. When their disagreement is reported to the Buddha, he resolves it by explaining that he expounds the Dhamma through multiple frameworks according to context—analyzing feelings into two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, or one hundred and eight varieties—and admonishes his disciples not to turn contextual expositions into causes of division [Carpenter 2014; Rogell 2003]. In a study of canonical verb morphology, MN 59 is classified among linguistically later discourses on the basis of its aorist forms [Kingsbury 2002].

The discourse then outlines a progressive hierarchy of pleasure or happiness (*sukha*), moving beyond sensory pleasures through the four *jhāna*s, the four formless attainments (*arūpa*), and culminating in the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*) [Saitanaporn 2009; Griffiths 1986]. A distinctive doctrinal feature of the sutta is that each successive meditative state in this ninefold sequence is characterized as a happiness more excellent and sublime than the preceding one (*sukham abhikkantatarañ ca paṇītatarañ ca*), explicitly reckoning even immaterial states and cessation under the rubric of happiness [Anālayo; Griffiths 1986; Polak 2011; Onians 2002].

MN 59 has a direct canonical duplicate in the *Vedanā Saṁyutta* at SN 36.19, as well as parallels in two Sanskrit fragments from the Turfan collection (SHT sutta 12 and sutta 79) and the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (SĀ 485). In the *Saṃyuktāgama* parallel, the setting is located in Rājagaha rather than Sāvatthī, and King Bimbisāra takes the place of the carpenter Pañcakaṅga as Udāyi's interlocutor [Klaus & Hartmann 2007]. Automated text-reuse data from DharmaNexus strongly corroborates these relationships, identifying extensive overlap with SN 36.19 (§1.3–6.3), alignments with the *Navakanipāta* of the Aṅguttaranikāya (AN 9.34) and other Pali collections, and cross-language alignments with Chinese Āgama texts (SĀ and MĀ) and later Sanskrit and Tibetan treatises [DharmaNexus].
